Babe Ruth revolutionized baseball in the nineteen twenties as the most dominant home-run hitter of his era, transforming the sport from a contact-hitting game into one centered on power. His charisma, larger-than-life personality, and prolific slugging made him the first genuine sports celebrity, and his twenty-seven seasons with the Yankees established the franchise as baseball's most storied dynasty.

He hit a record seven hundred fourteen home runs in his career, a mark that stood until nineteen seventy-four, and pioneered the modern power-hitting style that defines baseball today. In game three of the nineteen thirty-two World Series, he called his shot, allegedly pointing to the outfield before hitting a home run to that exact spot. Before joining the Yankees, Ruth played for the Boston Red Sox from nineteen fourteen to nineteen nineteen, and the Yankees' acquisition of him in a trade many credit with cursing the Red Sox for eighty-six years.

Beyond his power, Ruth batted a career three forty-two average with twenty-eight hundred seventy-three hits, and his on-base plus slugging of one point one six four remains one of the highest ever recorded. Nicknamed The Bambino and The Sultan of Swat, he embodied both artistry and raw power. Off the field, he was known for his wild lifestyle, drawing fans as much for his celebrity as for his performance. He finished his career with ten World Series appearances and seven championships, mostly with the Yankees. Lou Gehrig was his teammate and fellow Yankees titan, while Joe DiMaggio succeeded him as the Yankees' marquee power hitter and franchise icon.
